analysis.one_liner: Ends corporate tax deferral on overseas profits and tightens offshore tax loopholes.
analysis.headline: The bill was never taken up by the Senate Finance Committee and died without a vote at the end of the 114th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tax the foreign profits of U.S. corporations in the year earned, rather than waiting until the money is brought home — the current rule that gives companies an incentive to park profits offshore. It would also limit a tax break large oil companies claim for payments to foreign governments, treat foreign corporations run from the United States as domestic companies, curb interest-deduction games that shift profits abroad, and tighten rules against companies that reincorporate overseas to dodge U.S. taxes. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who would pay less because corporations that currently shift profits overseas would no longer be able to defer U.S. tax on them indefinitely.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Individual taxpayers and small domestic businesses

how_it_helps.text: Ends deferral, so U.S. corporations would owe U.S. tax on foreign profits in the year earned instead of waiting until the money is repatriated [S2, S3].
Denies the foreign tax credit to large integrated oil companies that are dual capacity taxpayers, closing a loophole related to payments to foreign governments [S2, S3].
Limits the foreign tax credit to income actually subject to U.S. tax, restoring a per-country approach [S2, S3].
Treats foreign corporations managed and controlled in the United States as domestic corporations for tax purposes [S2, S3].
Limits the interest-deduction for U.S. members of financial reporting groups with excess domestic indebtedness, curbing earnings-stripping [S2, S3].
Tightens rules for inverted corporations: acquisitions after May 8, 2014 would be treated as inverted if the foreign entity holds more than 50% of stock, a tougher test [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Multinational corporations, especially those with large foreign profits; large integrated oil companies; and companies that would otherwise reincorporate abroad.

drawbacks.text: Full taxation of foreign income on a current basis without a transition tax could complicate compliance and raise competitive concerns for U.S. firms operating abroad.
The bill's inversion test (80% ownership trigger) is a major tightening; some would argue it risks penalizing legitimate business combinations.
No companion House action occurred, and the bill never advanced past the Senate Finance Committee; there was no hearing or debate in this record.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets real tax-avoidance mechanisms that shift profits and taxes onto other taxpayers. Its main cost is compliance complexity and reduced tax planning flexibility for multinationals. The main weakness is that it died with no debate, so no formal cost analysis exists in the record.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Finance Committee for the rest of the Congress and never received a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Introduced by Sen. Sanders on April 14, 2015 and read twice, then referred to the Senate Committee on Finance [S1, S5].
No further action was taken after the referral; the Congress ended January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations, oil companies, and firms planning foreign reincorporations kept the existing tax rules in place, avoiding higher taxes on offshore profits.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing, markup, or floor vote for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was an independent caucusing with Democrats and the sole cosponsor was a Democrat; no Republican support appeared, and the Republican-led Finance Committee took no action.

industries.note: Would lose the ability to defer U.S. tax on foreign profits, closing a major profit-shifting avenue.
Would lose a foreign tax credit related to payments to foreign governments.
A tougher 80% ownership test would catch more deals as inversions.
